summary: Explains why peer-to-peer and other distributed applications can waste network resources by choosing peers without knowing the network layout. It sets out the problem Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) should solve: giving applications guidance about better choices. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you borrow a toy, it is smarter to ask a neighbor than someone across the world. ALTO helps programs learn which other computers are close by, so data takes shorter trips.

questions: why do p2p applications need network topology information
why do p2p applications waste bandwidth
what is the difference between local peering and transit traffic
subtitle: Why applications that pick peers at random waste network resources, and what a service that guides them should do.

tldr.problem: Distributed applications such as file sharing and media streaming pick peers randomly or from partial measurements, with little knowledge of the network underneath. That can cause congestion and costly traffic across network boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) problem: an information-sharing service lets applications make better-than-random peer selection, using slowly changing facts such as network proximity, location, costs and operator policy.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a protocol or a requirements document. It sets terms, use cases and issues such as privacy and topology hiding for later work.

facts.label: Scope of the ALTO client protocol
facts.value: Queries and responses between ALTO client and server

today: RFC 5693 is an Informational problem statement, published in October 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol and sets no standard.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
Distributed applications, both peer-to-peer (P2P) and client/server, use a significant amount of network capacity. They often have several replicas of a resource to choose from, but applications generally lack reliable information about the underlying network. They therefore choose among peers randomly or from partial observations. For example, measuring only round-trip time during connection setup cannot reliably show actual throughput.

The result can be traffic that crosses network boundaries many times, overloading links that are often congested and costing the network operator money. Studies cited in the RFC suggest a remedy: ISPs, network operators or third parties can collect more reliable network information, such as topology or link capacity, that changes on a much longer time scale than transport-layer congestion information. Both applications and operators have an incentive to share and use it.

The RFC says existing proposals consist of two parts: a discovery mechanism to find an information source, and a protocol to query it. It is not clear how they would perform if deployed globally, and wide adoption is unlikely without agreement on a common, open standard.
sections.eli5: Programs that trade files pick partners almost blindly, which sends data on long, expensive trips. If someone who knows the roads could tell them who is nearby, everybody would save effort.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC defines the roles in an ALTO exchange. A resource (such as a file or a media relay) is often available from several providers. A resource consumer needs it, a resource provider has it, and a resource directory (for example a P2P tracker) helps consumers find providers.

The ALTO service gives guidance on which provider to select. An ALTO server answers queries, and an ALTO client sends them. The client may be embedded in the resource consumer, in the resource directory, or both. An ALTO query asks for guidance, an ALTO response carries it, and the pair is an ALTO transaction.

Three traffic types matter for ISP cost: local traffic stays within one ISP and is usually cheapest, peering traffic is exchanged between directly connected ISPs and is often free under the peering agreement, and transit traffic is paid for between ISPs. Of the protocols involved, only the ALTO client protocol is in scope. The application protocol and the provisioning protocol that populates the server are out of scope for the ALTO working group.
sections.eli5: There is someone who has the toy, someone who wants it, and a helper who knows who lives closest. Asking the helper and getting an answer is one ALTO conversation.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Network engineers have long worked on traffic optimization with mechanisms like MPLS and Diffserv, which find optimal routes or queues for packets between given addresses. Distributed applications cannot use these directly. When a P2P application connects, the target is not a stable host but a resource that may exist on many peers, and choosing a good host by topological proximity has a large effect on the traffic generated.

The RFC notes that traffic is not the only factor in user performance. Avoiding overloaded nodes and fetching rare file pieces first also matter, but better topology information still improves peer selection in an important respect. It helps most in the initial phase, when a peer or a streaming client gets a list of candidates and picks a smaller set. An economic goal for ISPs is to reduce transit traffic on interdomain links.

Addressing the problem has two sides: deploying an ALTO service that provides network information, and enhancing applications so they use it for better-than-random endpoint selection.
sections.eli5: Road crews can fix roads, but they cannot decide who you borrow a toy from. The program itself has to choose wisely, and it needs help knowing who is close.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists five areas where ALTO guidance could help.

  • File sharing: search results may show many instances of the same file. In Gnutella, selection is up to the user, so applications would need changes. In BitTorrent and eDonkey, central trackers or servers could implement it.
  • Cache and mirror selection: today this relies on inaccurate geolocation data, proprietary network-location systems, or the user's own choice.
  • Live media streaming: peers both receive and send content, and the goal is to find effective peers to exchange media with.
  • Real-time communications: NATs, firewalls or proxies may force media through relays with public addresses, and ALTO should help peers find the best relays.
  • Distributed hash tables: ALTO information can help DHT algorithms that keep a routing table of other peers.
sections.eli5: It helps when you swap files, pick the nearest download copy, watch a live stream together, make a video call through a helper computer, or look things up in a shared directory.

sections.title: Aspects of the Problem
sections.content:
Not every kind of information suits an ALTO service. Rapidly changing facts such as transport-layer congestion are out of scope, because they would be outdated or require constant contact, and end-to-end delay and available bandwidth are better measured by applications themselves. Suitable information is what applications cannot easily learn and what changes slowly: operator policies, geographical location, network proximity, transmission costs and remaining traffic quotas.

At least three kinds of entity can provide the service: network operators, third parties such as content-delivery networks or companies acting for ISPs, and user communities that estimate topology. Some communities expect a centralized ALTO server and others a distributed one, so some sort of service-discovery mechanism is expected.

Privacy cuts both ways. Clients that reveal their application type could get better answers, but may consider that information private. Operators often consider revealing topology details to be confidential. Caching and ALTO are orthogonal, and ALTO that is aware of caches can direct clients to nearby caches.
sections.eli5: Only slow-changing facts, like which town a computer is in, are worth passing along. Fast-changing ones, like traffic jams, are better noticed on the spot. Some people also do not want to share details.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is neither a requirements document nor a protocol specification, but it flags security and privacy areas that will matter for an ALTO design. Some environments may need client or server authentication, and the companion requirements document outlines minimum-to-implement security requirements. Digital rights management is out of scope.

Because applications may rely on ALTO information, the service provider gains influence over a system it was not part of before. The P2P community might consider an ISP-run server hostile if the operator could prevent content distribution to enforce copyrights, redirect applications to corrupted mediators, track connections for inspection or logging, or apply policies based on criteria other than network efficiency.

There is no protocol mechanism to require ALTO for P2P applications. If it fails to improve performance, it will not gain popularity. Users may be reluctant to disclose sensitive information and operators may not want to expose interior topology, so an ALTO protocol should not presume mandatory information disclosure by either side.
sections.eli5: If one company gives the directions, it could send you somewhere it likes better. That is why nobody should be forced to use it, and nobody should have to share secrets to get an answer.
